title: Polynomial orbit and factorial coefficients of an SL2 highest vector
statement:
Let $k$ be an algebraically closed field [def-weil-field, def-weil-algebraic-closure], of arbitrary characteristic. Write $\operatorname{SL}_2$ for the affine group scheme [def-sc-group-scheme] whose $R$-points are determinant-one $2\times2$ matrices over a commutative $k$-algebra $R$. Put $x_+(a)=I_2+aE_{12}$, $x_-(a)=I_2+aE_{21}$ and $h(t)=\operatorname{diag}(t,t^{-1})$, where $I_2$ is the identity matrix and $E_{ij}$ has its only nonzero entry $1$ in position $(i,j)$. Let $M$ be a finite-dimensional rational $\operatorname{SL}_2$-module, meaning a finite-dimensional $k$-vector space with a coassociative counital coaction into $M\otimes_k k[\operatorname{SL}_2]$. Let $m\ge0$ be an integer and $0\ne v\in M$ such that $x_+(a)(v\otimes1)=v\otimes1$ and $h(t)(v\otimes1)=t^m(v\otimes1)$ for every $R$, $a\in R$ and $t\in R^\times$. Let $f\in\operatorname{End}_k(M)$ be the differential of $x_-$, so that $x_-(\varepsilon)$ acts as $1+\varepsilon f$ over $k[\varepsilon]/(\varepsilon^2)$. There are unique vectors $w_0,\ldots,w_m\in M$ such that, for every $R$ and $a\in R$,
$$x_-(a)(v\otimes1)=\sum_{j=0}^m a^j(w_j\otimes1),\qquad w_0=v,\qquad f^jv=j!w_j\quad(0\le j\le m).$$
In particular, if $\operatorname{char}k=p>0$ and $m<p$, then every $j!$ in this sum is invertible in $k$, and the same orbit is $\sum_{j=0}^m a^j(j!)^{-1}(f^jv\otimes1)$. No simplicity assumption is made on $M$.

source.place: Agent rank-one consequence of Proposition 22.14 (polynomial root-subgroup orbit coefficients and their weights), Proposition 22.15 (Weyl symmetry of weights), Proposition 22.17 (weights of a cyclic primitive module), and the SL2 root and weight lattices in 22.33. Factorial recurrence follows by comparing the linear dual-number coefficient in x_-(a+epsilon)=x_-(epsilon)x_-(a).

proof.text: Write the coaction of $v$ as a finite sum $c(v)=\sum_i v_i\otimes g_i$. Substitution of the matrix $x_-(T)$ in each coordinate function $g_i$ gives an element $P(T)=\sum_{j\ge0}T^j w_j$ of $M\otimes_k k[T]$, with only finitely many nonzero coefficients. Evaluating $T\mapsto a$ gives $x_-(a)(v\otimes1)$ over every commutative $k$-algebra $R$. Similarly write $Q(S)=x_+(S)(nv)=\sum_{i\ge0}S^i z_i$, where $n$ has rows $(0,-1)$ and $(1,0)$. These are polynomial expansions of the given coaction, not an assumption about its differential.

source.place: p.466, paragraph preceding Proposition 22.14; direct substitution into the coaction.

proof.text:
For an invertible indeterminate $T$, direct matrix multiplication gives
$$x_+(T^{-1})n h(T)x_+(T^{-1})=x_-(T).$$
Indeed the first three factors have rows $(1,-T^{-1})$ and $(T,0)$; multiplying by the last factor gives rows $(1,0)$ and $(T,1)$. Apply the representation over $k[T,T^{-1}]$: the rightmost $x_+$ fixes $v$, and $h(T)v=T^m v$, by the hypotheses for this $k$-algebra. Therefore
$$P(T)=T^m Q(T^{-1})=\sum_{i\ge0}T^{m-i}z_i.$$
The left side has coefficients only in nonnegative degrees, while the right side has coefficients only in degrees at most $m$. Comparing the coefficients in the free Laurent-monomial expansion gives $w_j=0$ for every $j>m$.

source.place: pp.466–467, Propositions 22.14–22.17, rank-one big-cell coefficient argument written explicitly using 2 by 2 matrices.

proof.text: The inclusion $M\otimes_k k[T]\to M\otimes_k k[T,T^{-1}]$ is injective: after choosing a basis of $M$, it is a direct sum of the injective inclusion of ordinary polynomials into Laurent polynomials. Thus the degree conclusion is an identity already in $M\otimes_k k[T]$, and evaluation yields the required truncated orbit over every $R$, without requiring $a$ to be invertible. Evaluation at $T=0$ gives $w_0=v$ since $x_-(0)=I_2$. Any other proposed list giving the orbit for all $R,a$ agrees with this polynomial by taking $R=k[T]$ and $a=T$; comparison of coefficients proves uniqueness, including zero coefficients at the upper end.

source.place: p.466, Proposition 22.14, polynomial coefficients and constant term; universal-polynomial formulation.

proof.text:
In $A=k[T,\varepsilon]/(\varepsilon^2)$ the matrix identity $x_-(T+\varepsilon)=x_-(\varepsilon)x_-(T)$ and the definition of $f$ give
$$\sum_{j=0}^m(T+\varepsilon)^j w_j=(1+\varepsilon f)\sum_{j=0}^m T^j w_j.$$
Here $f$ acts $A$-linearly after scalar extension, and $x_-(\varepsilon)=1+\varepsilon f$ follows by extending its defining dual-number identity from $k$ to $k[T]$. Since $(T+\varepsilon)^j=T^j+jT^{j-1}\varepsilon$ for $j\ge1$, comparison of the coefficients of $\varepsilon T^j$ gives $f(w_j)=(j+1)w_{j+1}$ for $0\le j<m$ (and $f(w_m)=0$). This comparison is valid in every characteristic and divides by no integer.

source.place: Agent coefficient calculation from the lower-root addition law, supplementing Proposition 22.14, p.466.

proof.text: Induct on $j$ between $0$ and $m$. At $j=0$, $f^0v=v=0!w_0$. If $j<m$ and $f^jv=j!w_j$, linearity and the preceding recurrence give $f^{j+1}v=j!f(w_j)=j!(j+1)w_{j+1}=(j+1)!w_{j+1}$. If $\operatorname{char}k=p>0$ and $m<p$, each integer $1\le r\le j\le m$ has nonzero image in $k$ by the definition of characteristic. Their product $j!$ is therefore nonzero and has an inverse because $k$ is a field; $0!=1$ is also invertible. Solving for each $w_j$ and substituting into the already proved orbit identity gives the stated truncated exponential. No step uses simplicity of $M$.

source.place: Agent factorial induction from the dual-number recurrence; field and characteristic definitions.
